rules.title: Rule out body and basic needs before interpreting a refusal

context.text: Resident refuses or is distressed during care (washing, eating, instructions).

action.text: Run a somatic / basic-needs / sensory check (pain, feet and skin, hunger or thirst, hearing aids, glasses, noise) before choosing a behavioural explanation or intervention.

rationale.text: Unrecognised pain, discomfort, unmet needs and sensory deficits drive behaviour in people who cannot verbalise them; blaming the disease first misses the cause.

guardrails.text: Do not record a behavioural interpretation or a non-physical intervention for a refusal until a pain / physical-discomfort check is logged.

predicate.message: Pain / physical-discomfort check is not logged for this refusal.

sources.quote_span: First, clear everything that could be somatic, that could be related to the body, or the basic needs of the body.
Maybe that person is just not hearing me.
She's suffering in her feet. She's got edema. She's not wearing her compression stockings.
too much noise in the room, pain, etc.

rules.caution: The ~50% somatic-trigger figure is the expert's recollection, not a cited study.

rules.title: Review how care was approached; swap carer or call the psychologist before forcing care

context.text: Resident refuses with one carer on a given day.

action.text: Try a colleague with better rapport, or call the psychologist to de-escalate; document who intervened and what worked.

rationale.text: Rapport and the emotional climate of the interaction drive acceptance; refusals are often caused by how care is delivered.

guardrails.text: Never force care through a refusal; retrying unchanged with the same carer repeatedly is not a strategy.

predicate.message: Repeated refusal and the same approach is being retried unchanged.

sources.quote_span: I call in my colleague, and she doesn't get refusal, and the task is done.
it's the staff interaction with the residents.

rules.title: Repeated refusal goes to the team meeting; route by root cause

context.text: Repeated refusal (for example more than 3 times a day of eating or drinking).

action.text: Bring it to the daily team meeting; the team looks for the root cause (physical, psychological, or both).

rationale.text: Refusal is a symptom with heterogeneous causes; diagnosis precedes assignment.

guardrails.text: Do not close a repeated refusal alone: it must reach the team meeting. Revise the care plan only if the change is durable.

escalation.text: Physical cause: care staff (and doctor via nurse). Psychological cause without physical: psychologist, with activity staff.

predicate.message: Refusal has happened 3+ times today but nothing is escalated.

sources.quote_span: if it's severe enough, it would be brought up in a staff meeting
Any situation is either linked to your physical problem or a neuropsychological problem.

rules.title: Carers never change treatment; route via nurse, then coordinating physician

context.text: A medication or treatment change seems needed or is requested.

action.text: Raise it with the nurse; the nurse takes it to the coordinating physician, who speaks to the treating doctor.

rationale.text: Medical authority is distributed: treating doctors prescribe, the coordinating physician orchestrates, the home cannot direct external doctors.

guardrails.text: A carer does not give or change medication on their own judgement; medication changes remain a medical decision.

predicate.message: Medication is chosen without routing it to a nurse or physician.

sources.quote_span: when nurses raise something, [the coordinating physician] speaks to the treating doctors about adjusting treatment
Medication changes remain a medical decision

rules.title: Say whether the behaviour is new or habitual before escalating

context.text: A behaviour is about to be escalated.

action.text: Classify the behaviour as habitual or new first.

rationale.text: Whether a behaviour is new or habitual changes its meaning and urgency.

predicate.message: Escalating without saying whether the behaviour is new or habitual.

sources.quote_span: frequency, whether the behaviour is habitual or not

rules.title: Exit-seeking is not refusal: rework integration

context.text: Resident tries to leave, mostly in the first weeks after admission.

action.text: Review and intensify the integration plan; do not treat it as a refusal.

rationale.text: Exit-seeking expresses disorientation and lack of belonging; it fades with integration.

guardrails.text: Do not file exit-seeking under the refusal pathway or answer it with a refusal strategy.

predicate.message: Exit-seeking is being handled with a refusal strategy instead of an integration review.

sources.quote_span: It's just not the same approach, same strategy at all.
are very often people who are not sufficiently integrated into their home
